extracted.intended_audience: students and general readers of philosophy (those studying pragmatism and religious philosophy)
extracted.subtask_description: Lecture text (William James) presenting pragmatic criteria for meaning and truth, contrasting monistic and pluralistic religious interpretations, and outlining meliorism and pragmatic method for evaluating hypotheses. Aimed to clarify how philosophical hypotheses acquire practical meaning and religious significance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Pragmatic criterion of meaning and truth
rubrics_metrics.description: If the notion of a world ante rem ... can be shown to have any consequences whatever for our life, it has a meaning. The meaning will be true if the use squares well with life's other uses.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not treat universals as meaningless abstractions: test them by asking what concrete differences their acceptance would make in experience and life. A conception's truth is tied to its useful consequences and its compatibility with other working truths.

rubrics_metrics.name: Do not reject hypotheses with useful consequences
rubrics_metrics.description: On pragmatic principles we cannot reject any hypothesis if consequences useful to life flow from it.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate hypotheses by the practical benefits or uses they produce. Even if a hypothesis yields no scientific deductions, its emotional or spiritual use (e.g., Vivekananda's use of the Atman) can justify its acceptance within pragmatism.

rubrics_metrics.name: Pragmatic account of 'possible'
rubrics_metrics.description: When you say that a thing is possible, what difference does it make? A bare possibility means absence of real preventive grounds; a concretely grounded possibility means some of the conditions of production actually exist.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Analyze 'possible' by concrete, empirical conditions (example: a 'possible chicken' requires non-contradiction, absence of enemies, and an actual egg/incubator). The more conditions present, the better-grounded and more probable the possibility; when all conditions are complete, possibility becomes actuality.

rubrics_metrics.name: Meliorism as pragmatic attitude toward salvation
rubrics_metrics.description: Meliorism treats salvation as neither inevitable nor impossible; it is a possibility that grows more probable as the actual conditions of salvation accumulate. Pragmatism must incline towards meliorism.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Rather than absolute optimism or pessimism, adopt an attitude that acknowledges existing conditions for improvement and works to add complementary conditions through action. Interpret 'salvation' broadly (individual ideals realized contribute to world salvation).

rubrics_metrics.name: Interpretive criterion for poetry: monistic vs pluralistic readings
rubrics_metrics.description: A poem's exaltation of the 'you' (Whitman) admits two useful readings: (1) monistic/mystical—You are absolutely safe inwardly (quietism); (2) pluralistic—'You' as better possibilities or redemptive effects that set definite activities in motion.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prefer the pluralistic reading when emphasizing concrete future experiences and actions: it suggests an 'infinitely larger number of the details of future experience' and sets activities at work. Respect the monistic reading's historic validity but recognize pragmatism's sympathy for readings that produce concrete consequences.

rubrics_metrics.name: Acts as local creators of reality (pragmatic agency)
rubrics_metrics.description: Our acts, our turning-places, where we seem to ourselves to make ourselves and grow, are the parts of the world to which we are closest ... Why should they not be the actual turning-places and growing-places of the world?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Treat individual action as a genuine causal contributor to worldly change: evaluate moral and religious significance by the tangible effects of agents' acts. Anticipate rationalist objections (that growth must be integral), but give weight to 'living reason'—wishes and actions—as real reasons for events.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinguish rationalistic monism from empirical pluralistic unification
rubrics_metrics.description: Don't conflate taking the world's perfection as a necessary principle (monism) with taking it only as a possible terminus ad quem (pluralism). The former guarantees all good and makes bad impossible; the latter treats salvation as a contingent possibility grounded in particulars.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Be precise in terminology: 'rational unity' (abstract/necessary) differs from empirical 'unification' (possible/achieved through particulars). This distinction affects whether one seeks consolation in guaranteed wholeness or works toward improvement through concrete means.

rubrics_metrics.name: Pragmatism as mediator between tough-mindedness and tender-mindedness
rubrics_metrics.description: Pragmatism is offered expressly as a mediator between tough-mindedness (naturalism, rejection of eternal perfection) and tender-mindedness (rationalistic absolutism).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Adopt pragmatic temper if you seek a middle path: respect universal conceptions insofar as they have practical use, avoid extreme abstract absolutism, and avoid crude naturalism that dismisses values. Use the pragmatic test (what works) to reconcile competing temperaments.

rubrics_metrics.name: Religious hypotheses judged by whether they 'work' in the widest sense
rubrics_metrics.description: On pragmatistic principles, if the hypothesis of God works satisfactorily in the widest sense of the word, it is true. Religious experience can be evidence that higher powers exist and are at work to save the world on ideals similar to our own.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not dismiss theistic or superhuman hypotheses a priori; evaluate them by their experiential fruitfulness, moral and spiritual effects, and how they integrate with other working truths. Pragmatism allows religious belief if it produces life-enhancing results.

rubrics_metrics.name: Practical orientation to possibility and probability
rubrics_metrics.description: Possibility is to be understood in terms of existing conditions and the probabilities they afford; the more complementary conditions exist, the more probable and substantial the possibility becomes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When assessing plans, beliefs, or ideals, enumerate and weigh the actual conditions that would produce them; favor strategies that increase those conditions. This operationalizes abstract notions like 'possible' into actionable considerations.
